and when John Bostick in turn fell
heir to it, he cared for it as tenderly
as if it was one of his offspring.


The old chair has full swing of
ten feet and its motion is delightfully
easy, but it possesses one fault, and
that is, the two front legs are loose
in the rockers, and sometimes they
will fly out when the chair is on a
downward tilt and throw its con-
tents, irrespective of age or sex,
further than a bucking horse. Miss
Harper, who is circulator of scan-
dal, as well as an old maid, called on
Mrs. Bostick short time ago, and
seating herself in the chair, ex-
claimed, as she began rocking:


"Ooh! Mrs. Bostick, I just cropped
in to see if you had heard anything
of that dreadful report about Ella—"
Simmons' arm was seen around her
waist, and—" But the story was
cut short by a crash, and the next
moment the air was rent with
shriek and a pair of red hose, as Miss
Harper executed a back somersault
and landed violently on the floor
amid a chaotic mass of crinoline.
Bostick heard the shriek, and dashing
into the parlor saw a couple of at-
tenuated limbs waving frantically in
the air.


Not comprehending the true state
of affairs he beat a hasty retreat and
left his wife to meet the emergency
as best she could. He had faced the
glistening bayonet without a tremor,
but an old maid with the fits was
more than he could stand.


"John," said his wife, after Miss
Harper had revived and taken her
leave, "you must have the old rock-

ways afraid when any one comes to
see me that they will sit in it and get
hurt. Why, last week Deacon Pot-
ter called on me and about the time
he was giving me a great deal of
spiritual comfort the old rocking
chair flew up and pitched him
through the hearth screen."


"Nancy," said Bostick, "thought-
fully, that old chair was made in
my grandfathers' days, when people
were good and honest, and whenever
any one sits in it who isn't square it's
going to repudiate the load every
time. Now, Deacon Potter may be
a good man, but for all of that it
doesn't look well for him to begin
counting old Mrs. Dusenberry before
her husband has been dead a month.
I guess, Nancy, it is better to let the
old rocking chair remain as it is. It
will be a kind of safeguard when I'm
away."


For a moment his wife was ab-
sorbed in deep thought, and then her
face frightened and she inquired
meekly: "John, you remember Mrs.
Bedell, who is always caring for the
orphans, and who nursed you when
you was sick?"


"Why, certainly I do."


"She is a very good old lady, isn't
she?"


"Yes, Nancy, there isn't a better
old lady in Louisiana than Mrs.
Bedell."


"Well, she came to see me about—"

Marrs last evening under the auspices of the Young Men's Christian Association.

The subject was treated with mastery and, and the lecture was illuminated throughout by refined scholarship and true eloquence. It was instructive and entertaining, humorous and pathetic, plain, and yet brimming with strong logic, and finished with the adornments of classical rhetoric.

The lecturer replied to the recent sneers at oratory, and showed by the examples of such men as Demosthenes, Chatham, Mirabeau, Henry and others what eloquence has done in shaping the destinies of men and nations. He gave the names of Chrysostom, Spurgeon, Richard Fuller and other eminent divines as examples of the power of pulpit oratory to sway the passions and affect the hearts of men. He claimed that no age of the world was so favorable to oratory as the present, with the momentous questions now pressing themselves upon the public attention. He maintained that Reason, Imagination, Conviction and Action are the elements of eloquent oratory; but without them, eloquence is but a hollow shell. Calhoun possessed the eloquence of reason and logic; but he was a granite column. Milton possessed the magnificence of a winter's night when all the stars are out. Demosthenes said, "the time to build a monument has not come, but it will come." The oratorical powers were combined in him.

The lecturer, while admitting the advantage of crises and occasion to the orator, clarified that the essence of real eloquence is not merely the possession of oratorical gifts and graces, but the blessed quality of virtue. Bad men may be eloquent. Bolingbroke was eloquent; Ingersoll, the desperado of modern infidelity, is eloquent; Beecher is eloquent; the devil is eloquent; but virtue is the basis of all true eloquence.

The gifted speaker illustrated his lecture by several trite anecdotes, and carried his audience completely with him. Dr. Hawthorne has commanding presence and a remarkably fine physique. His voice is rich.

Allow me to submit to the legislature, especially the whole frontier delegation from Red river to the lower Rio Grande, the wisdom and justice of legislation on subject of very great future importance. In the law providing for the sale of alternate relations of common school lands, the asylum, state capital and all other reserved lands, insert distinct proviso that wherever large bodies of land may be enclosed for pasturage the owner or owners shall be required to allow the passage of public or county wagon roads through them and keen gates at the points of ingress and egress, the necessity for which shall be determined by the commissioners court of the county in which the land may be or of the county to which such county may be attached. The trouble in Arizona with the Indians is now directing public attention to the mismanagement of Indian affairs by our government. To say that our dealings with the Indians have resulted in a lamentable, miserable and disgraceful failure, so far as keeping them in a peaceable attitude towards us, is but voicing the opinions of nine tenths of the people of the Territories. Everyone who has resided east of the Missouri river for the last fifteen or twenty years will testify how utterly inadequate are the means adopted by the general government to preserve our frontiers from the invasions of the cruel, merciless foe. Montana has been retarded in her progress several years by their continuous outbreaks and depredations upon our people. Other and contiguous territories have also felt the injuries sustained to their several industries, to the development of their resources and to their material prosperity. Not only in these but in another and deeper respect have we suffered. Hundreds of true, noble and valued citizens have yielded up their lives as sacrifices to the ignoble, crafty assassins. Women have been virulently outraged; families most hidiously and vilely tortured; homes devastated and property destroyed and laid waste. We have seen all this, and at times too, when there was no general uprising among the Indians—when the agents reported that the tribes on their reservations were quiet and peaceable, and only out on such pursuits as hunting and fishing, and we have seen these same Indians, after perpetrating cold-blooded murders, return to their reservations and be received, as the prodigal son was received, with outstretched arms, and fed and pampered by the government until they were ready to make another raid upon the defenseless inhabitants of the surrounding country. This has been so often repeated and protection from the wrath of the outraged settler and immunity from the operations of the civil law extended to them that no one can be surprised at this last savage outbreak in Arizona. It is but the legitimate outgrowth of the policy of the government toward the Indians and so long as that policy shall continue just so long may such outbreaks be anticipated.

But how is this matter to be remedied is the question that naturally arises. There are those, and they comprise all those who have given the subject thought and careful study—who hold that the question can be solved only by turning over the care of the Indians to the War Department. An effort was made some time ago to effect this result. In the latter part of the forty-fourth Congress a bill was introduced and supported by the solid representation of the Pacific Coast, providing for the transfer of the Indians to the department named. Two objects could be gained by the enactment of this measure: First, the reduction of the expense of maintaining the Indians by dispensing with the vast number of agents and subordinate officials on the reservations, and second, by placing the military in such contact with the various tribes as to enable them to obtain information concerning their intentions and movements and check them when such movements would lead to a collision with the whites. Other advantages were also to be gained by the transfer which would have shown themselves in the better behavior of the Nations towards us. But there appeared to be a spirit of philanthropy born of ignorance of the Indian nature that had much to do in defeating the wholesome change. And then again there was a great aversion manifested against displacing agents, contractors, and a long line of greedy cormorants, of positions in which a systematic swindling of the government appeared to be permitted. However, the wishes of the people were disregarded, and the Indians were continued in charge of the Interior Department. To render the matter worse, the government has sent out men from the east as agents who are in entire ignorance of the Indian nature, and for whom the average Indian entertains supreme contempt. We may rest assured that as long as this policy is continued our frontiers will be visited by predatory bands of Indians, and settlers, to protect their own lives and property, will be compelled to organize, as they have in Arizona, and meet the savage on his own ground and in his peculiar manner of warfare. The patience of the long suffering frontiersman is becoming wildly exhausted, and unless the government can afford them better protection in the future than it has in the past, they will undoubtedly be forced to solve the Indian problem in a way that may result more disastrously to the Indian than would his transfer to the War Department.

In one of the Parisian Bureaus de Police
Correctionnelle, a few days ago, a hardy
man of toil, accused of stealing a pair of
trousers, was discharged by the sitting
magistrate, after long and patient inves-
tigation of his case, on the ground that the
evidence brought forward against him was
insufficient to ESTABLISH his culpability.


He continued, however, to keep his seat
on the prisoner's bench after his acquit-
tal had been formally pronounced. The law-
yer who had conducted his defense,
observing that he did not move, informed
him that he was free to go about his busi-
ness, if he had any. He shook his head
slightly, but did not budge. By this time
no other case being on hand, the court
was nearly empty. Again addressing him,
his defender inquired with some irritation,
"Why the deuce he did not get up and
go?" "Step this way, a moment, please,"
replied the steadfast sitter, "and let me
whisper in your ear. I can't go till all
the witnesses for the prosecution have left
the court. And why, may I ask?"


"Because of the stolen trousers—don't
you understand?" "What about the
trousers?" "Only this—I've got 'em on."

received from Mexico. According to a
journal which made the announcement,
Don Carlos has decided on taking up his
abode in that country with his wife and
children. Before arriving at this deter-
mination, the DUKE of Madrid prudentially
inquired whether his presence in Mexico
would be distasteful to the authorities. A
satisfactory reply was, however, soon
returned by telegraph to the effect that in
a free land like Mexico everyone was
welcome, provided that he did not con-
spire against the tranquility of the republic.
If the Mexican paper is correctly informed,
Don Carlos may therefore be expected to
settle ere long in a country which, es-
pecially to one of Spanish descent, presents
many features of interest.

barracks. Entrenching tools and lanterns have been
served out for the use of patrols in the event of
gas being cut off from any of the barracks. There
are now here 30 officers, 600 men, 100 horses
and 10 guns, the "Flower of the British Army,"
besides strong bodies of constabulary.


NEW YORK, Dec. 29.—The Commercial Bullet
has been informed by the Captain of the Escan-
bes recently arrived here from Bombay, that two
ocean steamships ordered by the China Mer-
chants Company, for service in the regular line
between China and San Francisco, will be finished
by next July, and will commence weekly service
from China in August. They will be manned by
native crews and commanded by English and
American captains. They are being constructed
at Glasgow, and will be only 1000 tons each. The
Captain believes that there will be ample emplo-
yment for these vessels.


CONSTANTINOPLE, December 29.—The Albania
League has summoned all males over eighteen
years of age to arms in every district in North
Albania. A great gathering at Jacova has ap-
proved war with Montenegro, and has decided
to send two mobiles to Cettinje to demand the
evacuation of Dulcigno. If Prince Nikita refuses,
the League is instructed to declare war on behalf
of Albania. The menacing attitude of Greece is
causing the Porte to take precautions. Two iron-
clads have sailed for this Archipelago, and the
fortifications of the Dardanelles are being
strengthened.


NEW YORK, December 29.—The Times say
there is something like panic in English poli-
tical circles, caused by the threatened war betwee-
n Russia and China. The failure to settle a
boundary dispute, the responsibility for which clearly
rests with the Government at St. Petersburg,
gives color to the suspicion that Russia has sought
occasion to quarrel with China for the purpose of
provoking war of conquest, and that the ultimate
result of the impending disturbance will be the sub-
jugation of the Chinese and the opening of
a Russian highway across the Celestial kingdom
to the waters of the China seas. English news-
papers bristle with descriptions of the Russian
naval vessels now on the way to the coasts of
China and Japan. The whole array is said to
be a powerful fleet armed with new rifle guns of
force and range yet unmatched in naval warfare.


NEW YORK, Dec. 30.—The Herald's London ed-
itorial says: Professor P. Harding, of the Universi-
ty of Utrecht, Holland, has drawn up an address
to the British nation, praying for the re-establish-
ment of the national independence of the Dutch
Boers of the Transvaal. The address is being
numerously signed in the Netherlands.

on Saturday received a telegram from
one in New York offering to wager $600
that the cotton crop of 1881 will
exceed six million bales. The proposi-
tion was announced in cotton circles,
and there was a rush to take up the
proposition, some proposing to make up

man receiving the dispatch declined to
let any one in, but telegraphed back that

urging the party to make it $4,000.


Kinston Journal: Mr. J. C. Kennedy
reports that he has made this year
on 15 acres of his poorest land at least
$500, net profit. This poor land was
sown in oats last winter, and owing to
the unfavorable spring for small grain,
not a very good crop was gathered.
After the oats were cut off he applied
a coat of cotton seed turned under and
thoroughly harrowed, and from it he
has just housed over $400 worth of fine
hay, including the value of the oat
crop. In cutting the hay he used a
mower and rake, thereby saving consid-
erable in the way of labor. Mr. Ken-
nedy says all his best land was put in
cotton and pretty well manifold, and
while this 15 acre lot of poor land has
paid him such a handsome profit it is

most of our farmers this year, whether
there will be any balance to the credit
side of the cotton farm.

WASHINGTON, May 13.-The Republican
caucus met this forenoon, but the Senators
were slow in reaching the capitol on account
of hot weather. Hardly more than half of
the Republican Senator's were present. Talk
was resumed on about the same line as the
last caucus, viz that the Republican Senator's
will.do all they can to prevent any bad feeling
over the Robertson case; that they will en-
deavor to settle it without leaving any sting
to follow. The proceedings were interrupted
by a session of the Senate, aud it was under.
stood that the caucus wonld meet this after
noon, unless executive business should keep
the Senate in session too late. No definite
plan appears to have been agreed upon, but
several Senators say they were encouraged by
a conference this morning to hope that sat
isfactory adjustment may yet be affected.


MATTHEWS SAFE.


No motion or suggestion of reconsidering
Stanley Matthew'S case was made in executive
session to-day, and the confirmation now
stands as final and secure.


POSTPONED.


The Republican caucus which adjourned
subject to call of the chair did not meet again

Friends, Countrymen, LADIES, and Gentlemen,—I am thrice happy in the circumstances under which YOU have called upon me.

The eloquent and beautiful address to which you have listened has been so full in its recital as to require no addition. Your honored guest and orator, General Fitzhugh Lee, rode with Stuart in his perilous campaigns, shared his trials and dangers, took part in his victories, was the equal of his commander, and became the worthy successor of that immortal chieftain. When the Army of Northern Virginia made its last march to Appomattox Courthouse, a numerous foe lowering on his flanks and rear, "little Fitz" was there with the remnant of his cavalry to do and dare, and, if need be, die for Dixie. How vain it would be for any one to add to what has been said by such witness.

Again, and lastly, Jackson's character and conduct so filled the measure of his glory that no encomium could increase or adorn it. When he came from the academic shades of the Virginia Military Institute, what military fame to which the quiet professor would reach? He rose with the brilliancy of a meteor over the blood-stained fields of the Potomac, but shone with the steady light of the orb of day—a light around which no evening shadows gathered, but grew brighter and brighter the longer it shone. It is not alone by us that his merit has been recognized. In Europe, so far as I had opportunity to learn, he was regarded as the great hero of our war, and appreciative men in England have contributed the bronze statue to him, the first and only one which they have given to one of our soldiers. The column which stands before me, crowned with a statue of enduring stone, which you have reared to commemorate his services and virtues, is fit tribute from you, and teaches useful lesson to posterity, because it is erected not to perpetuate the story of his military prowess merely, but also, and perhaps even more, to record his pure patriotism, his piety, and private worth. No place could have been more appropriate than this for such a testimonial, for the fame of Jackson is closely identified with the heroic history of Louisiana.

In the beginning of the war the Confederate states were wanting in all the material needed for its prosecution, and there was nothing which was more difficult to supply than field batteries. From the first battle of Manassas, where Jackson won his sobriquet of Stonewall, in the East and in the West, the guns of the Washington Artillery were heard wherever battles were fought. In the ever memorable campaign of the Shenandoah, where Jackson with the swoop of the eagle attacked the divided columns of the enemy, and, beating them in succession, drove his vast host from our soil, the sons of Louisiana were a staff on which he securely leaned.

This was to gain position on the mountainside, above the enemy's most effective battery, and descend to attack him in flank and enfilade. After Taylor had put his troops in motion he went to receive from Jackson his final orders. He found him in front of his line of battle, which had just been forced back. Marshall, September 24—Last night about half-past 11 o'clock, bloody tragedy was enacted at the Gem saloon in this city. The facts are as follows: W. L. Phillips, a printer, resident of this city, and A. B. McNeely, an employe of the Texas & Pacific Railroad company, were playing at the faro table. They both had stakes on the board. The coroner's jury rendered their verdict substantially as follows: "The jury find that A. B. McNeely, came to his death last night about half past eleven o'clock at the Gem saloon, in this city, by being cut in the breast with a knife by Phillips, and that the killing was without cause and unprovoked by Phillips." As soon as made aware of the condition of this man skipped but up to this time has not been arrested. McNeely was a comparatively stranger, but represented to be a harmless, quiet man. The theft was perpetrated by a young man in no way connected with the company. ticipated danger from the enemy un-
less it might be in the shape of
some small band of guerrillas lurk-
ing amid the mountain gorges, ac-
tuated more by the hope of plunder
than by patriotic motives. There is
little twilight, you know, in the
tropics. The sun had disappeared
in the folds of an immense cloud
which was rapidly spreading itself
over the entire heavens, while from
its sable depths darted lurid sheets
of lightning, followed by the increas-
ing roar of thunder which had al-
ready found an echo through the
valleys and gorges of the mountain.


I did not fancy wet jacket, and,
whistling for my dog, was on the
point of retracing my steps down
the rough mountain road when the
jingling of spurs and accoutrements,
the trampling of horses and the
hoarse word of command was suf-
cient for me to draw back into a tall
tuft of grass growing beside me.
A number of Mexican lancers were
before me preparing to bivouac for
the night, and my retreat down the
road was out of the question.
High, precipitous rocks hemmed me
in on three sides, through which the
road I had travelled had been orig-
inally cut. The outlet was now in
possession of the lancers, while in
front of me the steep side of the
mountain, verging almost to preci-
pice, sloped towards the city. To
remain where I was would be only
to court death, a nameless fate, an
unknown grave, for discovery was
certain to follow when the sentinels
should be posted.


I cautiously examined the smooth
sides of the precipice, covered here
and there by a network of vines
clinging to the crevices and rifts in
the rock for its uncertain life.
Further on I beheld a dark, irregu-
lar line disappearing in the murky
depths below, which proved to be a
deep, dry gully, the channel of
some mountain stream long since
dried up. Dropping my fowling-
piece and bidding my noble dog to
shift for himself, I swung myself
over the precipice, clinging to the
network of vines which shook and
complained beneath my weight.


The darkness had increased with
astonishing rapidity, and as I
swung over that rayless void I
found it impossible to pierce the
gloom. I heard the short, sharp
howl of my dog as he darted off in
search of me; then, amid the rush
of the squall, came the confused
shouts of men, struggling; shot
or two mingled with the crash of
the heavy artillery rolling in the vast
expanse above me. Depending
principally upon the strength and
endurance of my arms, I carefully
and cautiously felt my way along
the verge of the precipice, working
in the direction of the gully, which,
once, rained, promised to afford me
the means of escape from the dan-
gers which encompassed me.
Broad sheets of lightning lit up
with dazzling distinctness the fear-
ful scene, bringing out every un-
dulation of the rocks, every crevice
and blade of grass; once when I
found a slight support for my feet,
and was giving my aching arms a
rest, I glanced above amid the yell-
ow glare of the lightning and
beheld the fierce dark-whiskered
face of a Mexican, peering over the
brink, his eyes apparently fastened
upon me as I hung suspended and
flattened against the cliff but a few
feet below him, while the electricity
twisted and writhed like tongues of
internal serpents around the muzzle.

grounds for the opinion professed to be held
by the signers of a certain petition, who were

meant in this instance "called or invited" to
give their reasons for holding these opinions.

ical opinions, based upon personal examina-
tion, were given, except that was altered by Dr.
Webb." This is the statement of the Advert-
iser, and we venture to assert that no state
ment more intentionally, willfully, consciously,
the EXTREMIST departure from truth, was ever
printed. No medical opinions, based upon
personal examination—What do the medical
gentlemen say? Dr. McKibbin says as the
Advertiser very well knows, "I saw Polua at

with him." Then follow the particulars of
the conversation with him and with the officers

he is in perfectly sound mind there is no

committed the deed." DR. Brodie: At re-

the dross."

envy whenever she meets Lily in her
elegant gown; and the Grenvilles
never tire of boasting of "the Ellises—
our cousins, you know!"

Like heirs apparent in hereditary monarch
les, the Vice Presidents of the American Re-
public appear to drift instinctively into oppo-
stion even when they are not named, in order
to appease the weaker of two hostile factions
within the party OF our vice presidential
Presidents, Tyler was the first He was chos-
en- in 1910 on the Wing ticket with General
Harrison, who was sixty nine years old when
he was inaugurated. Within few weeks af-
terward h. died from the effects of cold
caught while going to market in a truly DEM
ocratic fashion one raw March morning. He
fell victim to an over estimate of his constitu-
ton and physical powers, and not unwarned
by his friends, whose kindly suggestions were
not only unheeded, but seemed to annoy him.
He Law i'll in the White House only nine days
He was the first President who died in Office
His leath was an astounding shock to the
whole country, and when the people awoke to
the fact that another person whom they had
elected Vice President, and whom they knew
only as "Tyler too had become President,
there went up a universal and anxious query,
"Who is he-what sort of man is hep" But
the death of Harrison had been anticipated
several days before it happened. Tyler, VINO
was then at his home on the Potomac Penin-
sula, WAS sent for Immediately in Govern
ment steamer. He took the oath quietly and
priyately General Hsrrison's cabinet concur
ded that Mr. Tyler while performing the func-
tons of President, ought to bear the title of
"vice President acting President" but Mr..
TYLER, under the advice of Chief Justice Ia
new, at once assumed the full presidential
title He announced that he would retain the
Harrison cabinet, of which Daniel Webster
was Secretary of State. The Harrison-Tyler
Wings were in doubt and dismay, for Tyler
had been put on the ticket with the knowledge
that he was rather an erratic member of the
party. Within three months Mr.. Tyler vetoed
two fiscal measures of his party in Congress
looking to a destruction OF the Van Buren, sub
treasury system and to the re-establshmaDt OF
national bank. By the 18th Of September
what turned out to be final rupture between
the new President and the Wing party began
with the resignation of all the cabinet except
Mr. Webster who did not remain much lon
ger. The new cabinet was composed of NOM
inal Wings, but all the congressional Wings,
except Henry A. Wise and Caleb Gushing, de-
serted Tyler after the Wing congressman had
issued in the autumn of 1911 a celebrated man
ifesto drawn up by John p. Kennedy of Mary
land, calling for caucus committee, OF which
Kenneth G. Rayner, now in Government en-
ploy in Washington, is the only survivor.
From that time forward Tyler received his
main support frem the Democrats.


General TAYLOR was the second President
who died in office. He died in the month of
July. Only five days before his death, on In
dependence day, General Taylor had attended
the exercises at the Washington Monument.
These lasted above an hour, during which the
President, with the obstinacy of an old cam
paigner in the tropics refused to shelter him
self from an uncommonly hot sun even with
an umbrella Exhausted and overheated on
his return To the White House he ate cherries

rison, was expected for many hours before it
occurred. Immediately after that event the
cabinet officers addressed official letter to
Vice President Fillmore, giving him official
notification of the vacancy, of which in his
turn he gave official notice to the houses of
Congress, then in session over the compromise
measures He informed Congress that he
should take the oath as President on the same

as tine cabinet of General Garfield has mani

VICE PRESIDENTS

Like heirs apparent in hereditary monarchies, the Vice Presidents of the American Republic appear to drift instinctively into opposition even when they are not named, in order to appease the weaker of two hostile factions within the party. Of our vice presidential Presidents, Tyler was the first. He was chosen in 1840 on the Whig ticket with General Harrison, who was sixty nine years old when he was inaugurated. Within few weeks afterward he died from the effects of cold caught while going to market in a truly democratic fashion one raw March morning. He fell victim to an overestimate of his constitution and physical powers, and not unwarned by his friends, whose kindly suggestions were not only unheeded, but seemed to annoy him. He lay ill in the White House only nine days. He was the first President who died in office. His death was an astounding shock to the whole country, and when the people awoke to the fact that another person whom they had elected Vice President, and whom they knew only as "Tyler" had become President, there went up a universal and anxious query, "Who is he—what sort of man is he?" But the death of Harrison had been anticipated several days before it happened. Tyler, who was then at his home on the Potomac Peninsula, was sent for immediately in Government steamer. He took the oath quietly and privately. General Harrison's cabinet concurred that Mr. Tyler while performing the functions of President, ought to bear the title of "Vice President acting President," but Mr. TYLER, under the advice of Chief Justice Taney, at once assumed the full presidential title. He announced that he would retain the Harrison cabinet, of which Daniel Webster was Secretary of State. The Harrison-Tyler Whigs were in doubt and dismay, for Tyler had been put on the ticket with the knowledge that he was rather an erratic member of the party. Within three months Mr. Tyler vetoed two fiscal measures of his party in Congress looking to a destruction of the Van Buren sub-treasury system and to the re-establishment of national bank. By the 18th of September what turned out to be final rupture between the new President and the Whig party began with the resignation of all the cabinet except Mr. Webster who did not remain much longer. The new cabinet was composed of nominal Whigs, but all the congressional Whigs, except Henry A. Wise and Caleb Cushing, deserted Tyler after the Whig congressman had issued in the autumn of 1841 a celebrated manifesto drawn up by John P. Kennedy of Maryland, calling for caucus committee, of which Kenneth G. Rayner, now in Government employ in Washington, is the only survivor. From that time forward Tyler received his main support from the Democrats.

General TAYLOR was the second President who died in office. He died in the month of July. Only five days before his death, on Independence day, General Taylor had attended the exercises at the Washington Monument. These lasted above an hour, during which the President, with the obstinacy of an old campaigner in the tropics refused to shelter himself from an uncommonly hot sun even with an umbrella. Exhausted and overheated on his return to the White House he ate cherries and died ill. President Taylor's death, like that of Harrison, was expected for many hours before it occurred. Immediately after that event the cabinet officers addressed official letter to Vice President Fillmore, giving him official notification of the vacancy, of which in his turn he gave official notice to the houses of Congress, then in session over the compromise measures. He informed Congress that he should take the oath as President on the same day. It was administered in the hall of the House onto which the Senate had also gone by the venerable chief justice of the district, Cranch, in the extraordinary way of Mr. Erastus Brooks. Mr. Fillmore simply took the oath, but made no address, and after taking it retired. General Taylor's cabinet showed as unfriendly disposition towards Mr. Fillmore as the cabinet of General Garfield has manifested towards Mr. Arthur. No favor he had ever asked had ever been granted. He had recommended two persons as collector and postmaster at Buffalo, where he resided. Not only were they not appointed; the places were filled with Seward or Anti-Slavery and not Fillmore Silver Gray Whigs. As soon as Fillmore became President, Mr. Clayton, Secretary of State, sent in his resignation, and Daniel Webster was appointed in his place. A few days afterward an entirely new cabinet was made in which Mr. Fillmore's law partner and intimate friend and adviser, Nathan K. Hall, was placed as Postmaster-General. Thereafter during Mr. Fillmore's Administration the breach between the Stalwarts of that day (the Seward Anti-Slavery Whigs) and the Half-Breeds of that day (the Silver-Grays) widened continually. The party which elected Fillmore hated him as intensely when he retired as Tyler had been hated. The administrations of these two Vice Presidents prepared the way for the successes of the Democrats in the election of Polk who succeeded Tyler, and of Pierce who succeeded Fillmore.

The third of our Vice-Presidential Presidents, Andrew Johnson, took the oath as President as quietly and privately as Tyler had taken it. His quarrel with the Republicans was not of such sudden and rapid growth as the quarrels of Tyler and Fillmore with the Whigs but it became in the end quite as irreconcilable, radical and bitter. Johnson's differences with his old party leaders, like those of Fillmore, grew out of his refusal to wage war politically upon the South. Like Tyler, Johnson formally joined the Democratic party before he left the White House, and like Tyler he sought, but sought in vain, a nomination from Democratic national convention.

us. Among the most formidable of these the
roads, some of which are in horrible and almost
impossible condition. Although we are best

not get our claims properly presented before the
powers-that-ne at the county seat. The reason of
this is apparent to every one-they fear decapita-
ton 1t would be a great blessing to some of the

useful and blessing to the neighborhood in

of the roads to the Board, have competent men
to attend to them, and MT persist in forcing the
taxpayers in the rural districts to pay their
money without providing them with passable
highways for getting their products to market
eve would like to say just here that the above

borhood would be benefited by such society.

stand, when it is a known fact that during the

tion. It would be a great blessing to some of the
rural districts if this were done. Instead of being
useful and a blessing to the neighborhood in
which they are supposed to work the roads, they
become a very expensive nuisance that could well
be dispensed with. That these luxuries under-
stand their business all will admit, especially pedestrians,
who find the sidewalks well drained to
the gutter which is generally called the centre
of the road. But we are looking for better things
after the promised visit of one of our Commis-
sioners, who will no doubt present the true condition
of the roads to the Board, have competent men
to attend to them, and not persist in forcing the
taxpayers in the rural districts to pay their
money without providing them with passable
highways for getting their products to market. (We
would like to say just here that the above
promise was made prior to the election.)


Protracted meetings in order. We
could mention some six or eight within radius
of many miles. We expect to join in, soon
the repairs at the old Union completed,
when all supervisors are invited.


We heartily agree with "Random," the old
"bean raiser," in regard to organizing literary or
debating societies. We claim that every neigh-
borhood would be benefited by such society.
But in many localities there is no place for hold-
ing such meetings, except the school houses. This
the school laws forbid. Why the patrons are de-
barred their use for such purposes we don't under-
stand, when it is a known fact that during the
late campaign some of them were used for holding
political meetings. Will some those in authority
please rise and explain, and by so doing oblige
many patrons, among them, your humble servant,


CLAUD D.

Mr. INGALLS, offered a resolution for a committee of three Senators to sit during the recess of the Senate for the purpose of inquiring into the state of the law relative to the adjustment of pensions, with authority to report at the next session of the Senate, by bill or otherwise, what measures are necessary to secure early adjudication of all applications for pensions. Ordered printed and laid on the table.

Edward Everett, written after his retirement from the office of Secretary of State, in reply to Lord John Russell on the proposed tripartite convention relating to Cuba. Senator Donehoo at last amended it by
adding "whenever the work shall be-
come so large in the estimation of the
clerk as to demand the assistant."
Adopted.


On motion of Senator Dennis, two
were appointed (Dennis and Woods) to
wait on the Governor and receive any
papers from his hands, and inform him,
in conjunction with like committee
from the House, that the Legislature
was ready for work.


Senator Brown presented S. B. No. 1.
Its title is Authorizing copy of a deed or
other writing to be admitted to record
under certain circumstances.


Communications were received from
Secretary of State Brady, announcing
the returns as in from all counties ex-
cept WAYNE. A paper was also read
announcing a contest for the seat of Sena-
tor Smith by James Furbee. All were
referred to the Committee on Elections.


Messrs. Grantham, Monroe and Nor-
row, reported that the House was ready
for business.


Senator Farnsworth moved that the
Senate adjourn until 10 o'clock this
morning, and that action had
been taken and some of the
members had left the chamber
when Mr. Speaker from the House
appeared with H. J. No. 1, providing
for the counting of the vote of the last
election as provided under the acts of
1877. President Summers quickly called
the body to order, the Sergeant-at-Arms
was sent out to bring in members, and
on motion of Senator Brown it was de-
cided to apologize to the committee from
the House, by saying "the Senate had
supposed the House to be engaged in
the lowly work of electing pages."


The Senate concurring in the resolu-
tion, under a suspension of the rules,
Senators Newman and Stolling were ap-
pointed to inform the House of this ac-
tion.


Senator McGregor presented resolu-
tion that was adopted, asking the Presi-
dent to invite the clergy to open the ses-
sions with prayer.


The Senate then took a recess until 5
p. m. on motion of Senator Brown.


Afternoon Session.
President Summers called the Senate to
order at 5:05 and Senator Brown pre-
sented his colleague Senator Barbee of
Mason who was duly qualified.


Messrs. Leonard, Morrow and Sea-
bright of the House, appeared and stated
that that body was ready to count the
vote cast at the State election and re-
quested the presence of the Senate.
The Senate accompanied these gentle-
men to the Delegates Hall.


On reassembling at p. m. on motion
of Senator Brown, the Senate adjourned
until 10 o'clock this morning.
